narrative:
The model predicted a 60.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability exceeded the school's acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. Placing in the second decile is noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted. Your first-year ranking in the second decile similarly pulled the outcome toward rejection, though its effect was smaller.

Your LSAT score of 42 worked in the opposite direction. This score is higher than the average of 37 among accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction toward passing. However, the positive influence from your LSAT was not large enough to overcome the downward pressure from your class rankings.

Taken together, these academic signals led the model to conclude that the risk of bar exam failure was too high for admission. Gender, race, family income bracket, undergraduate GPA, and planned full-time status played no meaningful role in the outcome.

To improve your chances in future applications, focus on strengthening your academic performance and class standing. Raising your grades in law school and improving your position in the class rankings would have the largest positive impact on similar predictions. Consider retaking the LSAT only if you can reach a substantially higher score, and explore schools with different admission thresholds.
